Dashboards are central to contemporary organizations aiming to ‘datafy’ decision making and management practices. As one of the primary media through which people engage with digital data in organizational contexts, dashboards shape how data is accessed and perceived. Despite their ubiquity, there is limited understanding of how dashboards mediate data visibility and influence observers’ perceptions of the data. Drawing on theories of mediation and diagrammatics, this paper analyzes the ‘generic form’ shared by all dashboards. It then identifies the modes of observation encouraged by dashboards, revealing how they position their observers. While grounded in theoretical arguments, the analysis incorporates empirical examples from a study on the datafication of Human Resource Management. The paper makes two key contributions. It emphasizes the critical role of visual forms in datafication processes, and it highlights the organizational implications of the use of a specific kind of visual medium: the dashboard.

Shared e-scooters are now common in urban transportation, but safety planning remains limited by a lack of exposure-based, spatially detailed crash risk measures. This study applied an exposure-based approach to identify high-risk e-scooter corridors in Nashville, Tennessee, combining 92 police-reported, motor-vehicle-involved e-scooter crashes with trip-kilometer exposure data over a 45-month period. Crashes were assigned to corridors by rider direction of travel, and rates were calculated per 100,000 vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) citywide and by corridor. Across more than five million e-scooter kilometers of exposure, the citywide crash rate was 1.84 per 100,000 VKT, and 82.6% of crashes occurred at intersections or driveways. The 25 corridors accounted for 75.0% of crashes and 70.9% of VKT, with a combined rate (1.94 per 100,000 VKT) statistically indistinguishable from the rest of Nashville (1.58; p = 0.34). Corridor-level rates were nonetheless heterogeneous (chi-square = 96.17, df = 24, p < 0.001), with unadjusted rates ranging from 0.69 to 24.49 crashes per 100,000 VKT; empirical Bayes shrinkage reduced this spread to roughly 3.7-fold. Three corridors, Shelby Avenue, 21st Avenue, and West End Avenue, exceeded the citywide rate individually, with the first two remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Exposure-adjusted corridor rates gave a different picture of risk than crash counts alone: citywide averages concealed substantial street-level variation, supporting corridor-level exposure measures as a screening tool for micromobility safety, though individual designations remain exploratory rather than confirmatory. These results let agencies combine trip and crash data to target safety investment at high-risk corridors.

Background Digital technologies have changed how work is paced, monitored and bounded. Studies of technostress and related digital demands differ in what they treat as the exposure and the outcome, and in their evidence on processes, boundary conditions and organisational responses. Methods We searched Scopus, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library and Springer Nature on 3 September 2026 for English-language empirical studies published from 2010 to 2026 that linked a work-related digital stressor to employee well-being. Study quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings were synthesised by vote counting based on direction of effect, without meta-analysis. The review was not registered. Results Of 2,742 records, 353 full-text reports were assessed and 80 were included (78 quantitative non-randomised studies, one mixed-methods study, one experiment), with about 95,900 participants. Seventy reports pointed to poorer well-being (87.5%; 95% confidence interval 78.5% to 93.1%), eight pointed in conflicting directions and two to better well-being. Among reports of a demand, the share ranged from 72.2% for positive well-being to 95.7% for recovery and sleep, and was 76.3% in larger and 97.4% in smaller studies. Three studies that separated the demand from technology use found the adverse association for the demand only. Process and moderation tests (57 and 45 reports) gave selective support, and lagged tests gave mixed results. No report evaluated an implemented organisational response; 62 offered recommendations only. Certainty of the evidence was rated very low. Conclusions Digital demands experienced at work are associated with poorer employee well-being in most studies, though less uniformly in larger and better-controlled ones; the association appears to belong to the demand, not to technology use as such. Evidence for processes is largely cross-sectional, and evidence for organisational responses is absent.

Generative-AI learning systems typically centralize conversational information in one agent or use multiple agents primarily as tutors or collaborators. This study presents a distributed multi-agent generative-AI architecture in which role-specific AI non-player characters (AI-NPCs) act as bounded information sources with private evidence states. The architecture was implemented in an information-verification serious game and evaluated with 90 first-year undergraduates randomly assigned to classroom instruction, a single-agent AI game, or a distributed multi-agent AI game. The two AI configurations used the same cases, total information, verification resources, GPT-5.1 model, generation settings, scoring rules, and final task; the principal difference was the information-access architecture and its associated interaction demands. All conditions produced substantial digital-literacy knowledge gains, with no significant differences in transfer accuracy. The multi-agent condition outperformed classroom instruction in source evaluation, evidence integration, and reasoning quality, and significantly exceeded the single-agent condition only in evidence integration. It also showed more frequent investigative actions. These findings suggest that controlled information distribution across generative-AI agents can influence information-seeking and evidence integration even when the underlying model and available information are held constant, supporting bounded agent states and controlled information asymmetry as interaction-design mechanisms for information verification.

Background AI feedback holds promise for supporting student learning, but unstructured use can lead students to passively accept AI-generated answers, weakening their independent reasoning. This study examined whether structured AI feedback affects undergraduate students' critical thinking, learning performance, and engagement in a data science analytics course. Methods An exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study was conducted in a three-month undergraduate data science course (N = 167). One class received four-phase structured AI feedback, while the comparison class received conventional instructor feedback. Propensity score matching was used to improve comparability on observed baseline characteristics. Critical thinking was assessed using an adapted 40-item assessment covering five dimensions. Results Students receiving structured AI feedback demonstrated higher post-test critical thinking scores than matched controls, with a baseline-adjusted difference of 5.64 points (95% CI [3.62, 7.65], p < 0.001). A significant between-group difference in pre-to-post changes was also observed. Dimension-level analyses revealed significant differences in Evaluation of Arguments, Interpretation, Recognition of Assumptions, and Inference, while Deduction showed no significant difference. Higher learning performance, cognitive engagement, and behavioral engagement were also observed in the structured AI feedback group, whereas emotional engagement did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusion The findings provide exploratory evidence of differences in critical thinking and learning outcomes between the structured AI feedback and conventional instructor feedback classes. They highlight the potential relevance of feedback designs that encourage students to actively evaluate, question, and revise AI-supported analytical work, while underscoring the need for further studies that can isolate intervention-specific effects.

documents.abstract: Elite strength and conditioning (S&C) coaches occupy a critical but underexamined position as first-line users of sports-science technology, responsible for translating raw athlete-monitoring data into immediate training decisions. Through seven semi-structured interviews with elite S & C coaches across NCAA Division I, professional, and Olympic contexts, we identify four recurring breakdowns in their daily data work: fragmented vendor ecosystems, metric overload, scale and staffing constraints and staff turnover. Static mockup elicitation during interviews revealed a consistent preference for simple, interpretable interfaces that foreground selected metrics and concise explanations over dense data displays. We position elite S&C coaches as a distinct user group whose needs are poorly served by current systems, and propose four design priorities: integration stability, selective metrics with contextual explanation, scale-aware views, and governance continuity, to guide future coach-facing sports-science interface design.

Industrial production plants in sectors such as chemicals, life sciences, metals and mining, pulp and paper, and power generation operate with a high degree of automation. During steady-state operation, control systems maintain process stability with little need for human intervention, while operators primarily supervise plant behavior and intervene during startup, shutdown, product transitions, or abnormal situations. At the same time, modern plants must monitor multiple domains simultaneously, including process performance, asset conditions, cybersecurity threats, and physical security. These developments significantly increase the number and diversity of events generated by monitoring systems. Advances in sensing technologies, connectivity, and data analytics have greatly improved the ability to detect deviations from normal operation. However, the increasing volume of anomalies detected raises the challenge of determining which events should be brought to the attention of human supervisors. Since direct human intervention becomes less frequent but more critical in highly automated plants, the effective use of operator attention becomes an essential aspect of system design. This paper examines monitoring within the broader framework of supervisory control in industrial systems. Monitoring is viewed as the continuous determination of system state across multiple domains, with anomaly detection forming the basis for subsequent supervisory decisions. Building on this perspective, the paper analyzes how detected deviations are translated into events and discusses criteria for deciding which events require human attention. A structured view of monitoring and supervision is proposed that integrates process operation, asset health, cybersecurity, and physical security. The goal is to outline event generation design principles supporting effective human oversight in increasingly autonomous industrial environments.

Decision support systems (DSS) have evolved through a sequence of recognizable generations: data-driven systems built on query and reporting technologies, model-driven systems built on optimization and simulation, knowledge-driven systems built on encoded expertise, and, most recently, intelligent DSS (IDSS) that embed machine learning (ML) within the decision process. Across all four generations, one architectural constant has held: the human retains the final act of choosing and implementing. This chapter argues that agentic artificial intelligence, meaning systems that autonomously plan, invoke tools, retain memory across episodes, and execute multi-step courses of action, constitutes a fifth and qualitatively distinct generation of decision support. This fifth-generation classification is advanced as a conceptual proposal grounded in, but not established by, the reviewed literature. The claim rests not on improved predictive accuracy but on a structural relocation of Herbert Simon’s intelligence-design-choice-implementation cycle from the human to the machine. The gap is empirically visible: a synthesis of 2,093 ML-in-DSS papers found that only 43 (about 2%) addressed the implementation phase of decision-making, which is precisely the phase agentic systems now enter. The chapter extends Onwujekwe and Weistroffer’s four-layer IDSS development framework into an agentic architecture, proposes a taxonomy situating agentic DSS along axes of autonomy, decision horizon, reversibility, and oversight, illustrates the taxonomy across four application domains, and confronts the open problems of evaluation, auditability, goal drift, and oversight economics. The chapter follows a literature-based conceptual review approach, and an evidence matrix maps its major claims to supporting sources and evidence type.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

Designing Knowledge Management Systems (KMSs) for higher education requires addressing complex human–technology interactions, especially where staff turnover and changing roles create challenges for reusing knowledge. While advances in process mining and Generative AI enable new ways of designing features to support knowledge management, existing KMSs often overlook the realities of educators' workflows, leading to low adoption and limited impact. This paper presents findings from a two-year human-centred design study with 108 higher education teachers, examining iterative co-design and evaluation of GoldMind – a KMS supporting in-the-flow knowledge management during digital teaching tasks. Through three design–evaluation cycles, we examined teachers' task-evaluations and how feedback informed refinements. Insights are synthesised across three themes: (1) Technology Lessons from user interaction data, (2) Design Considerations shaped by co-design and usability testing, and (3) Human Factors, including cognitive load and knowledge behaviours, analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (in the last iteration). This study demonstrates that embedding human-centred, workflow-integrated KMSs can improve task efficiency, reduce cognitive load, and support knowledge reuse, while shaping educators' knowledge management behaviours through context-aware and proactive support. However, findings are based on a single-institution, controlled evaluation, limiting generalisability and requiring longitudinal, in-the-wild studies to assess adoption and impact.

Background Digital gamification has become an important instrument for mobilizing public pro-environmental behavior, yet many policy-driven sustainability platforms still face a retention problem: initial curiosity often fails to develop into sustained commitment. Objective This study integrates Self-Determination Theory and Flow Theory to explain how gamified contest design sustains engagement in China’s Carbon Generalized System of Preferences. Methods Drawing on survey data from CGSP participants, we combine partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results The PLS-SEM results show that task challenges enhance autonomy and competence satisfaction in the voluntary CGSP context, while socially embedded feedback strengthens relatedness satisfaction. These need states foster flow experience, an important proximal predictor of sustained engagement. The fsQCA results identify three equifinal configurations for high engagement, indicating that sustained participation can arise through different combinations of design features and psychological states. Conclusion These findings offer practical guidance for designing low-carbon platforms that move beyond short-term incentives and support durable public participation through psychological pathways.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly playing a role in learning, information work, and decision-making. The present study examines whether how people use GenAI matters more than how often they encounter it. In a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 350 GenAI users, usage intensity (years of use, weekly frequency, and daily duration) was distinguished from functional AI reliance (using AI instead of completing a task independently). Cognitive dependence, self-efficacy, critical thinking, and decision-making were analysed as separate outcomes, with cognitive dependence also tested as an indirect-path variable and response checking as a moderator. Usage intensity was not a significant predictor in the final models. Adding response checking and functional reliance jointly increased explained variance, with the largest unique contribution coming from reliance for cognitive dependence (ΔR²=.366) and self-efficacy (ΔR²=.072), and from response checking for critical thinking (ΔR²=.241) and decision-making (ΔR²=.026). Functional reliance was positively associated with cognitive dependence (β=.611, p<.001) and self-efficacy (β=.271, p<.001), negatively associated with critical thinking (β=−.117, p=.007), and not significantly associated with decision-making (β=.027, p=.626). Indirect effects through cognitive dependence were observed for critical thinking (ab=−.1316, 95% CI [−.1971, −.0668]) and self-efficacy (ab=.0829, 95% CI [.0247, .1468]); for decision-making, the negative indirect effect (ab=−.0917, 95% CI [−.1630, −.0192]) opposed the positive direct path and the total association was non-significant. The linear-ordinal moderation model showed a significant AI reliance × response checking interaction for decision-making (B=.0978, p=.012), but the small increment (f²=.017) and sensitivity to how response checking was specified warrant cautious interpretation. Because the design is cross-sectional and the principal outcomes are self-reported, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects or demonstrated changes in cognitive ability.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

documents.abstract: Project-based learning (PjBL) is common in computing education, but traditional assessments of PjBL often fail to capture higher-order thinking (HOT), especially in transfer contexts. This study introduces ''design problems'' (DPs): concise, scenario-based prompts that require applying project concepts in new situations, to address this gap. We examined instructor perceptions, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate DPs, and student experiences. Surveys of 31 instructors, evaluation of 80 LLM-generated DPs, and student performance data showed that while instructors value DPs, creation effort is a barrier. LLMs helped by producing high-quality prompts with strong expert agreement. Students rated DPs from different LLMs similarly, and their performance on DP tasks showed negligible correlation with traditional project grades, suggesting DPs may capture distinct aspects of HOT. Keystroke data also suggested deeper cognitive engagement of students through planning and revision behaviors. Overall, DPs appear to be a useful complement to traditional assessments, especially in situations where AI use or collaboration may undermine individual learning.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts analyses, builds models and recommends decisions, placing it at the centre of how managers diagnose and solve problems. This paper argues that the most serious risk of this shift is less the errors AI makes than cognitive offloading, defined as the delegation to an AI system of cognitive work that a manager would otherwise perform, and made measurable through four dimensions: extent, depth, verification and consequence. Using a transparent integrative review of 62 sources organised into six documented evidence strands, the study integrates the Paul-Elder critical thinking model, design thinking, dual-process theory, stages of automation and research on automation bias, and distinguishes generative AI from conventional rule-based automation and predictive analytics. A consolidated table of 20 empirical studies gives a mixed and conditional picture: AI raises immediate performance and, when designed to prompt and challenge, can support reasoning, but unguided use tends to weaken learning, verification and independent judgement. Studies of Kenyan entrepreneurs and Nigerian universities show that these effects are already visible in African settings, where infrastructure and capacity constraints raise the stakes. A comparative analysis of corporate strategy and finance, Nigerian higher education administration and the public sector shows how stakes, accountability and existing safeguards shape offloading risk. The paper proposes the Augmented Critical Thinking Cycle (ACTC), which embeds human-first gates in each design thinking stage, reserves problem framing for humans, applies the Paul-Elder standards as a verification layer and adds organisational guardrails. Implementation guidelines include decision tiers, a decision checklist, a phased roadmap and low-cost options for resource-constrained institutions, and seven testable propositions are offered. As a companion to an earlier study of management communication, the paper concludes that AI makes managers faster by default; whether it makes them weaker thinkers depends on how organisations design work around it.

documents.abstract: Near-miss events in the workplace serve as important signals for occupational accident prevention, and organizational responses to near-miss reports may influence employees’ perceived organizational support (POS). the association between organizational response patterns to near-miss reports and POS has not been sufficiently examined. This longitudinal study used data from an online cohort study of Japanese workers conducted at baseline (March 2023) and follow-up (December 2023). The analysis included 1,168 non-managerial workers who had experienced at least one near-miss event. Participants were categorized into four groups based on reporting behavior and the adequacy of organizational responses: reporting with adequate response, reporting with partial response, reporting with no response (reference), and no reporting. Associations between response patterns and POS at follow-up were examined using linear regression analysis. Employees in the reporting with adequate response (B = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.71–3.61) and reporting with partial response (B = 1.68, 95% CI: 0.12–3.23) groups showed significantly higher POS at follow-up compared with the reporting with no response group. The no reporting group also showed significantly higher POS (B = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.13–3.12). No significant moderating effect of company size was observed. These findings suggest that the quality of organizational responses to near-miss reports is associated with POS regardless of company size. Employees who reported near-miss events but received no organizational response showed the lowest POS, even lower than those who did not report. These findings highlight the importance of adequate follow-up and communication after near-miss reporting.

documents.abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.

Adaptive interfaces can reduce immediate information demands by postponing explanations, yet postponed material may remain essential for subsequent human oversight. This paper develops a theoretical framework for bounded explanation deferral in human–intelligent systems integration. It distinguishes an invariant decision-critical information layer from deferrable supporting material and treats the latter as a review obligation with an owner and deadline. A deterministic capacity balance connects present information demand, accumulated explanation debt, recovery opportunities and uncertainty about available attention. Analytical reasoning establishes a necessary cumulative feasibility condition and shows why deferral alone cannot resolve persistent demand. A transparent six-window worked example illustrates how scheduled repayment can remove temporary capacity exceedances while clearing deferred material before a dependent decision. Counterexamples demonstrate failure under insufficient recovery capacity, underestimated reading effort and misclassified critical evidence. These are mathematical illustrations, not participant observations or validated performance effects. The contribution is an auditable specification for adapting information timing while preserving contestability and identifying when operational escalation is required. The framework yields falsifiable propositions for later human-subject evaluation without assuming that lower workload necessarily improves safety.

When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.

documents.abstract: Against a backdrop of accelerated knowledge renewal, rapidly changing job requirements, and increasingly demanding performance standards, continuing education has become an important means for employees to maintain professional competence and for organizations to sustain competitive advantage. Yet demanding work contexts do not necessarily strengthen employees' continuing education participation tendency. Drawing on person–job fit theory, this study defines person–job fit as employees' evaluation of the compatibility between their abilities and job requirements. It examines how three role stressors—role conflict, role ambiguity, and role overload—relate to continuing education participation tendency among employees in for-profit enterprises through this fit evaluation and whether proactive personality moderates the relationship. A three-wave time-lagged survey yielded 335 valid matched responses. When the three role stressors were entered simultaneously, each significantly and negatively predicted person–job fit. Person–job fit significantly and positively predicted continuing education participation tendency and produced significant indirect effects between each role stressor and this tendency. Proactive personality significantly strengthened the positive relationship between person–job fit and continuing education participation tendency. By incorporating continuing education participation tendency into role-stressor research, this study identifies a cognitive appraisal pathway through which role stressors relate to a future-oriented developmental learning tendency and clarifies the boundary role of proactive personality.

documents.abstract: Nearly hundred studies in different times and places have documented that self-employed people report higher levels of subjective well-being than employed people. This “entrepreneurship well-being premium” is typically interpreted causally—"being your own boss" enhances well-being via more autonomy …

AI tutoring systems can provide timely, personalised feedback on programming tasks at scale with increasing number of GenAI-based programming tutors successfully generating course-relevant feedback through pedagogical guardrails and course-aware retrieval. A key challenge in such systems is ensuring appropriate reliance on AI output, neither dismissing useful guidance nor accepting fluent but incorrect suggestions. Accuracy alone does not guarantee uptake, as evidence suggests that students may discount feedback they know to be AI-generated. In this paper, we frame this as a trust calibration problem; how feedback is presented and how well learners can judge when to rely on it is as consequential as the feedback itself. We present SHIELD (Secure Helper for Intelligent Education and Learning Developments), an LLM-based tutor designed through the Human-Centred AI (HCAI) theoretical lens, embedding aspects associated with Oversight, Comprehension, and Integrity as key design properties. In a preliminary exploratory study with five undergraduate students, participants generally perceived SHIELD responses as more actionable and trustworthy than feedback from a plain RAG-based baseline. These findings concern perceived trustworthiness and call for further studies to establish trust calibration and system efficacy.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how human resource management (HRM) strategies are used to strengthen the leadership capabilities of cadres in the sub-district branch board (PAC) of IPNU–IPPNU, the Nahdlatul Ulama student and youth organisations, in Buaran District, Pekalongan Regency, Indonesia, and how these strategies shape cadre engagement. Design/methodology/approach: A descriptive qualitative case study was conducted. Data were gathered through interviews with the chairs, members and alumni administrators, observation, and organisational documents, and were analysed with the Miles–Huberman–Saldaña interactive model. Findings: HRM operates through three linked stages (strategy formulation, implementation and evaluation) embodied in a tiered pathway of MAKESTA, LAKMUD and DIKLATAMA, closed by follow-up plans (RTL) and monthly meetings. Recruitment, interview-based selection and placement, four forms of training (skill, retraining, cross-functional and creativity training) and reward–sanction mechanisms convert membership into leadership practice. A shift from quantity to quality coincided with a decline in cadres from about 90 to 48, while administrators rose from about 120 to 140. Cadres reported higher motivation, enthusiasm, leadership skills and belonging, although participation remained uneven. The study proposes the Sustainable Cadre Management Cycle for Leadership (SCMC), an eight-stage model. Research limitations/implications: The single-case design and reliance on self-reported accounts limit generalisation; the four propositions advanced here require comparative and mixed-method testing. Practical implications: Youth organisations can treat every programme as a leadership laboratory by sequencing training, delegated responsibility, follow-up and participation monitoring. Originality/value: The study integrates cadre management and leadership development into one cycle grounded in an under-researched faith-based youth organisation.

In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

documents.abstract: Background Pancasila Education combines conceptual understanding with civic and ethical learning. The design of digital course materials should respond to learners’ stated needs without treating media preference as evidence of educational effectiveness. This study describes students’ and lecturers’ needs for an interactive e-module at Universitas Riau, Indonesia. Methods A descriptive institutional needs assessment was reported using the newly supplied Indonesian questionnaire and aggregate tables. The student instrument contains 26 questions on learning perceptions, teaching methods, media, e-module features, and technology access. The available tabulations cover 442 students and 47 lecturers. Counts and source percentages were examined descriptively; sampling procedures, raw observations, questionnaire-to-table coding and psychometric documentation were unavailable. Results Among students, 365 (82.6%) selected interactive video and 351 (79.4%) selected e-modules as preferred learning media. Instructional videos (416; 94.2%) and interactive quizzes (406; 91.8%) were frequently requested e-module features. A strong need for an interactive e-module was recorded for 301 students (68.2%). All 47 lecturers were tabulated as needing an e-module, although the corresponding lecturer questionnaire was not supplied. The internet-access categories total 482 responses against 442 students and are not interpreted. Conclusions The tabulations inform tentative priorities for interactive Pancasila Education resources, especially explanatory videos, formative quizzes, case-based activities, and accessible mobile delivery. They do not establish e-module effectiveness or improvement in civic character. Sampling, instrument-to-table mappings, and numerical inconsistencies require further verification.

Avoiding loss-of-control events will be key to industry and society as AI technology is employed in various critical processes. In this article, we assess a hypothetical instability situation of an AGI − a singularity event − from a safety science standpoint. We present one way to describe the process of how a real time Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in its interaction with the environment may set it in a runaway condition. Our goal is clarifying general and structural control issues of strong real time AI for design, safeguarding and legislation. In cybernetics, instability and hence, the risk of loss-of-control, is a core trait of all highly adaptive systems. Such adaptive behavior can manifest as radical reframing – a pivotal process of a system that enables it to solve very hard challenges, and which requires it to redefine its core concepts, goals, values, plans and procedures. What emerges is the AGI power dilemma ; a double-bind between performance and controllability of a real time system. We discuss the consequences for human control of AGI and prospects for safeguarding when optimizing for power and speed. Moreover, we conclude that the human in the loop approach gives an illusion of safety when the AI is optimized for power.

The purpose of this quantitative, causal-comparative study was to determine if there is a difference in undergraduate college students’ generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) acceptance based on GPA levels when controlling for academic self-efficacy. This study matters because research indicated that GenAI may positively affect learning outcomes, including student engagement, improved learning attitudes, and enhanced academic performance. However, undergraduate college students using GenAI may not adopt or accept the technology in their learning. The sample comprised of 113 undergraduate students from institutions of higher education. This study combined three instruments to collect data. This quantitative study used the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) scale (Davis, 1989), the General Self-Efficacy Scale (Jerusalem & Schwarzer, 1995), and a demographic survey to collect data. A one-way Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) was conducted to determine the effect of undergraduate GPA levels (>1.0-2.0, >2.0-3.0, >3.0-4.0) on the transformed TAM scores while controlling for self-efficacy scores (GSE scores). The results revealed that the null hypothesis failed to reject at p < .05 that there is no significant difference in GenAI acceptance for undergraduate students as measured by the overall score on the transformed TAM based on GPA levels (>2.0-3.0, or >3.0-4.0) when controlling for academic self-efficacy as measured by the General Self-Efficacy Scale. Future research should include a larger, more diverse sample and use a longitudinal design that follows students across multiple semesters or academic years, with repeated exposure to GenAI, to examine changes in GenAI literacy and academic self-efficacy as students become more proficient in using GenAI.

documents.abstract: Objective Over recent decades, global adolescent wellbeing has deteriorated, with around 13.4% of adolescents worldwide meeting diagnostic criteria for at least one mental disorder. Although physical activity enhances adolescent wellbeing, the mechanisms driving this effect remain only partially understood. This systematic review examines whether basic psychological need satisfaction (BPNS—autonomy, competence, relatedness) mediates the relationship between exercise and wellbeing among 10–18-year-olds. Methods We systematically searched five electronic databases for peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026. In total, 23 studies met our inclusion criteria; these studies were narratively synthesized, assessed for risk of bias via design-appropriate tools, and collectively encompassed over 10,000 adolescents from 13 countries. Results Elevated BPNS was consistently linked to higher subjective vitality, greater life satisfaction, increased positive affect, and enhanced flourishing (β = 0.19–0.80; r = 0.19–0.68). Competence satisfaction emerged as the most reliable predictor of wellbeing, especially in competitive sports, while autonomy and relatedness impacts varied by context. Psychological need frustration independently associated with negative affect and burnout, supporting the dual-process model. Evidence is most robust in school physical education contexts, with notably scarce research on mindfulness-based and resistance training. The only included cluster-randomized controlled trial reported no significant intervention effect, and reliance on observational designs constrains causal inference. Conclusion This review highlights BPNS—especially competence satisfaction—as a credible mechanism linking exercise to better adolescent wellbeing. Thus, physical education curricula, youth sports initiatives, and exercise programs should adopt need-supportive approaches. Future RCTs must pre-specify BPNS as a mediator to confirm causal pathways. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261460142, identifier CRD420261460142.

With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), AI note-taking has become an important learning support tool for knowledge integration and thinking development, yet it is still mainly viewed as an efficiency-enhancing supplement to traditional note-taking. Therefore, understanding the factors associated with learners’ behavioral intention (BI) to use AI note-taking tools is important for promoting AI-assisted learning. Based on self-determination theory (SDT), this study examines the associations of processing fluency (PF) and learning agility (LA) with learners’ BI to use AI note-taking tools, as well as the moderating role of cognitive load (CL), in online learning environments. A total of 380 questionnaires were collected, and 308 valid responses were retained after data screening. Structural equation modeling was used for analysis. Results showed that PF and LA were significantly and positively associated with perceived autonomy (PA), perceived competence (PC), and perceived relatedness (PR). PA, PC, and PR were significantly and positively associated with BI. However, PF and LA showed significant indirect associations with BI only through PC and PR, whereas the indirect associations through PA were not statistically significant. Furthermore, CL scores moderated several first-stage associations. The positive associations between LA and PA and between PF and PC were stronger at lower CL scores than at higher CL scores. Given the context-specific and positively scored CL measure, these findings indicate variations in the associations across CL score levels rather than differences between higher and lower overall cognitive load.

Background: Conversational AI systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for reflection, planning, and everyday decision-making, emerging as potential instruments for human-agent collaboration. However, how to ensure relevance and quality, and collaborative behaviour of such systems is an open question, particularly in health-related contexts. Objective: The objective was to identify design requirements for developing an LLM-based collaborative diary agent supporting reflection and planning through dialogue grounded in a person’s activities and motives, which could serve as an instrument for diary studies in the future. Methods: An activity-theoretical framework was used for interpreting the collaborative diary construction activity. A participatory design methodology was applied involving six occupational therapy experts. Data were collected in co-design sessions through interviews and observations of prototype use, and data was analysed using inductive content analysis. Results: The findings highlight the importance of grounding, personalisation, explainability, emotional safety, ownership of diary content, and adaptive interaction in human-agent collaboration. The experts identified potential roles for the diary agent in revisiting experiences, supporting reflection, and planning everyday activities. The study also identified tensions between reflection and planning, structure and flexibility, and guidance and autonomy, interpreted as contradictions within the activity-theoretical framework. Conclusion: The findings suggest that diary-agent design should support the person in actively influencing and questioning generated narratives rather than simply automating narrative generation. Grounding, explainability, user control, and adaptability emerged as important requirements for future human–diary agent collaboration.

Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve. Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

documents.abstract: This cross-sectional study examines associations between the frequency of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) use, cognitive autonomy, and academic engagement among students at Félix Houphouët-Boigny University in Cocody, Côte d’Ivoire. Self-determination theory provides an interpretive framework. In May 2026, a structured questionnaire was administered to 400 convenience-sampled students from the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences who had previously used GAI for academic purposes. Descriptive statistics, Pearson’s chi-square tests, and Cramér’s V were computed using SPSS. Among these GAI users, 81.3% reported frequent use. Use frequency was associated with cognitive autonomy (χ²(4) = 19.847; p = .001; V = .158) and academic engagement (χ²(4) = 30.622; p < .001; V = .196). The association between cognitive autonomy and academic engagement was stronger (χ²(4) = 87.792; p < .001; V = .331). These cross-sectional associations do not establish causal effects. The findings support the need for critical pedagogical guidance and further investigation of how students use GAI in practice.

documents.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractHigher education institutions face mounting pressure to sustain lecturer engagement amid increasing workloads and constrained resources, yet the mechanisms underlying engagement formation remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to investigate how job resources and value alignment predict employee engagement among university lecturers in Indonesia, examining the mediating roles of employee well-being and affective commitment. A cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling was conducted in November 2025 with 272 full-time lecturers from 77 higher education institutions across five regions of Indonesia (Sumatra, Kalimantan, Java, Nusa Tenggara–Bali, and Sulawesi) using an online structured questionnaire. Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM via WarpPLS 8.0 with 999 bootstrap resamples. Work–life balance and job autonomy significantly predict employee well-being. Person–organization fit strongly predicts affective commitment; perceived organizational support does not have an effect. Affective commitment is the dominant predictor of engagement (R² = 0.631); employee well-being does not retain direct significance in the full model. Only the indirect path of person–organization fit → affective commitment → engagement is significant (β = 0.290, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.194, 0.386]), constituting complementary partial mediation. Servant leadership moderation is not supported. Robustness checks with demographic controls confirm the pattern of significant predictors is unchanged. These findings indicate that engagement is predicted more decisively by value alignment and emotional attachment than by exchange-based support, though generalization is bounded by the convenience sampling design.

The development of logical thinking is a core competency in STEM education that assessments identify as lacking in the High School Program. Compounding this gap is an emerging phenomenon: the tendency among students to rely on generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools to solve problems and submit answers without conducting their own analysis—a pattern of cognitive offloading that recent literature associates with the erosion of critical thinking and the loss of judgment. This article presents a methodological guide that uses video game programming with Python and the Tkinter library to strengthen logical reasoning in High School students, with the simulation of projectile motion serving as the central focus. The proposal is grounded in constructivism, Kolb’s experiential learning theory, and active learning methodologies, and is organized as design-based research, reporting on the design and internal validation phase of a prototype. The instructional sequence progresses through sixteen modules that guide students from basic syntax to a cannon simulator with real-world physics. It is argued that positioning the student as a producer of logic—who breaks down problems, encodes the physical model, and debugs their own errors—constitutes a deliberate pedagogical counterbalance to cognitive offloading, because it restores the cognitive effort and productive challenge that the uncritical use of AI tends to eliminate. The expected learning outcomes, the formative assessment rubric, and the implications for educational policy are discussed.

Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Industry 4.0 technologies is transforming how organisations plan, operate, make decisions, and compete. However, the leadership models required to integrate AI into organisational decision-making effectively remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining how leadership is evolving in AI-enabled organisational environments and how these changes influence organisational performance globally. This SLR was conducted across four academic databases using a predefined Boolean search strategy. Following a PRISMA-aligned screening process, 63 studies were selected for analysis, including four earlier key studies identified through citation searching. The selected articles were analysed using thematic coding in ATLAS.ti according to six predefined themes: leadership transformation, decision-making attributes, leadership–AI interface, modus operandi, innovation and agility, and organisational performance. These themes were selected to structure the analysis around how AI reshapes leadership roles, decision-making processes, and organisational outcomes, directly aligning with the research intent. The findings suggest that the impact of AI on organisational performance is facilitated primarily through changes in leadership roles and decision structures rather than technological capability alone. AI increasingly reshapes decision-making processes, organisational coordination, and leadership responsibilities, creating hybrid human–AI leadership arrangements. The review identifies a key gap in existing literature, namely the lack of clear and practical frameworks for implementing hybrid human–AI leadership in complex organisational environments. To address this gap, the review synthesises its findings into an integrative Human–AI Leadership Configuration (HALC) framework, a typology of four human–AI leadership configurations, and six testable propositions, providing a structured foundation for both researchers and organisational leaders to better align AI capabilities with effective leadership and improved performance.

documents.abstract: This study develops and tests an employee-centered model examining how perceived AI explainability is associated with acceptance of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at work. It distinguishes three practical dimensions of explainability, including transparency, interpretability, and actionability, and examines whether trust in AI statistically mediates the associations between these explanation qualities and employees' willingness to use, rely on, and recommend GenAI in organizational tasks. This study employed a cross-sectional explanatory mixed-method design with 486 employees in China and 18 completed semi-structured interviews. Twenty-two seven-point Likert items were analyzed in SmartPLS 4 using reliability and validity assessment, structural path analysis, 5,000 bootstrap samples, effect sizes, and predictive diagnostics. The estimates indicate that transparency (beta = .249), interpretability (beta = .300), and actionability (beta = .292) are positively associated with trust in AI. Trust is strongly associated with employee acceptance (beta = .518) and statistically mediates the associations between all three explainability dimensions and acceptance, with the direct paths remaining significant. The model explains 48.8% of the variance in trust and 58.1% of the variance in acceptance. Interview findings further show that employees value explanations most when they reveal uncertainty, support verification, and preserve meaningful human control. These results represent statistical associations, not evidence of temporal or causal mediation. The study advances workplace GenAI research by decomposing explainability into employee-relevant affordances and positioning calibrated trust as a mediating pathway between explanation quality and acceptance. The model and reviewed literature suggest that explanation design should not be evaluated by explanation volume alone; organizations should provide layered explanations that disclose limitations, make outputs comprehensible, and help employees check, correct, and appropriately contest AI outputs.

This exploratory descriptive study examines how university students report using generative artificial intelligence (AI) to prepare their contributions before sharing them with peers, and how they perceive its role in their confidence and motivation during team-based coursework. A 26-item online questionnaire was completed by 42 students at Ibn Tofail University, Morocco. Data was analyzed descriptively, and three multi-item scales showed good internal consistency (? = .80 to .86). All findings reflect students’ self-reported perceptions; no collaborative task was observed. Most students reported using AI often or always for academic work (69%) and in team projects (57.1%). Two-thirds (66.7%) reported at least one form of AI-supported preparation: rehearsing arguments, checking language, or checking whether an idea is sound. About half attributed greater confidence to AI, and between 50% and 64.3% reported motivational benefits. Only 21.4% felt less confident when peers used AI more effectively, whereas 66.7% said that teammates’ AI use motivated them, and 45.2% reported lower motivation when AI does too much of the work. The study identifies a preparatory stage of AI use that deserves attention from researchers and teachers.

There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.
